items.title: Marian McPartland — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Jimmy knew everybody. Like Red Saunders. Did you ever hear that name?

ctx.x: Was there much interaction with some of the black jazz artists on the South Side of Chicago, what group were there? At that point were there any integrated groups that were performing, or . . . at jam sessions, formally or . . .

There were. I never was aware of this whole thing. I was so naive. There was a guy there that used to promote . . . a young concert promoter. He promoted this concert with Jimmy on the one hand, and Bunk Johnson. I guess they brought him out of retirement and got him some new teeth or something. He played this thing. People flocked to see him. The concert was quite a success. After the concert, the two of them . . . Jimmy . . . he and Jimmy went off somewhere and got loaded. I lost . . . I never was that…

items.title: 70399_Theodore _Red_ Saunders oral history interview
items.q: Marian McPartland, all of those, they're very, very, very satisfied with what they--

ctx.x: So this is why you find all of these guys who come in here and they augment with them, like Teddy Wilson and -- well, Dorothy or whoever it is, if he comes in town, and they augment with them, from local musicians. They're very, very satisfied. Marian McPartland, all of those, they're very, very, very satisfied with what they--
I was talking to Milt Jackson last week, went down to hear him a couple of times. I was so -- and so was he and everybody else -- Teddy Edwards, --
